entities.name: Jacob of Mies
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jacob of Mies (Jakoubek ze Stříbra in Czech), a pivotal Czech theologian and reformer, became the leading intellectual voice for Utraquism after Jan Hus’s death, fundamentally shaping the trajectory of the Bohemian Reformation. Born in Mies (Stříbro), Bohemia, his life culminated in 1429, leaving an indelible mark on religious thought and political conflict. His most enduring contribution was the theological justification and practical implementation of communion in both kinds (sub utraque specie), advocating for the laity to receive both bread and wine during the Eucharist, a radical departure from established Catholic practice.

Following his studies at the University of Prague, Jacob of Mies emerged as a close associate and intellectual successor to Jan Hus. While Hus's primary focus was on moral reform and the authority of scripture, it was Jacob who, in 1414, independently initiated the practice of administering the chalice to the laity, a move that quickly became a defining feature of the Hussite movement. He eloquently articulated the scriptural and patristic arguments for Utraquism, defending it against condemnation by the Council of Constance and later by papal legates. His intellectual leadership was instrumental in formulating the Four Articles of Prague (1420), which codified Hussite demands, placing Utraquist communion alongside free preaching, clerical poverty, and punishment of mortal sins, thereby providing a theological and political manifesto for the burgeoning reform movement.
